newsitem.title: MEXICO: Salinas case adds to woes of Mexico justice system.
newsitem.headline: Salinas case adds to woes of Mexico justice system.

text.p: A federal appellate judge's ruling clearing Raul Salinas, the jailed brother of Mexico's ex-president, of tax fraud charges deals a fresh blow to the scandal-plagued justice system.

Late on Tuesday, Salinas won his first concrete break in a two-year battle with the government from behind bars when a federal appeals court judge dropped the tax fraud charges after finding there was too little evidence to convict him.
The ruling bolstered the impression that Salinas, who since his arrest on murder charges in February 1995 has been cast as the epitome of evil in Mexico, was undergoing an abrupt image resurrection.

During two years in jail, accusations against him have ranged from masterminding the assassination of the secretary general of the ruling party in September 1994 to illegally amassing some $150 million in foreign bank accounts while a public servant during the 1988-1994 administration of his brother, Carlos Salinas.

So far, no charges have led to a conviction, although Mexicans in general have seemed willing to accept that he was guilty. In recent weeks, however, that belief has been shaken, if not destroyed, by evidence of spectacular bungling in the attorney general's office that handled the cases against him.

"The abrupt change in the judicial situation of Raul Salinas can only be explained in two ways," La Jornada daily said in an editorial on Wednesday. "Either the institutions in charge of procuring justice were led during the last two years with extreme and unjustifiable ineptitude, or the charges against Raul Salinas ... were the expression of a persecution campaign with no legal basis."

The image of justice in Mexico took a fresh turn for the worse on Tuesday when the ex-attorney general who jailed Salinas, Antonio Lozano, said President Ernesto Zedillo was kept abreast of some of the questionable steps along the way.

Mexico's two main opposition parties have suggested that Zedillo's ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) may be pushing for an exoneration of Raul in order to rescue his brother Carlos, who fell into disgrace after leaving office in December 1994 and now lives in voluntary exile in Ireland.

With mid-term congressional elections scheduled for July, the PRI has also been barely able to hide its glee at the downfall of Lozano. A member of the National Action Party who was the only opposition member in the Cabinet, he was fired by Zedillo in December because of the embarrassing sluggishness of the case against Raul Salinas.

Lozano's fortunes sank to new lows last month when a new team of investigators discovered that a dead body dug up on Raul Salinas's ranch last October was planted there, apparently to sow false evidence against Salinas.

Lozano broke a virtual two-month silence late on Tuesday, holding a news conference to explain why he paid some $500,000 to a reputed witch and her cronies, who led his men to the body. He said such payments to witnesses were usual during an investigation and that Zedillo knew about them.

He emphatically denied the money was paid to the witch to plant the body and said any suggestions by investigators to that effect were part of a "lynching campaign" by pro-PRI investigators to discredit him and his party.
Zedillo's office immediately denied he had authorised the payments, but it fell short of denying he knew about them.

Reaffirming his belief that Salinas was guilty of all the charges against him, Lozano also urged investigators to follow up on allegations by the witch that Salinas had threatened her into planting the body to tarnish Lozano.

The attorney general's office said in a statement on Wednesday it continued "with utter firmness" the prosecution against Salinas on murder and other charges. But it made no mention of probing the witch's allegations.
